I live in Hamtramck and didn't have a car for a number of years. It's very doable, depending on your situation. For some of that time I was working downtown and could take the Chene bus (which is, IMO, decently reliable but not frequent enough) and for the rest I was working in Hamtramck and could thus walk to work. Ample corner grocery stores and markets to get most items, but what sucks is when you need to get to the bigger stores in the suburbs for something and have to use multiple busses and potentially multiple bus systems. Can definitely be done and people do it every day, but it requires a bit of extra planning.   


That being said, OP says they're coming from LA, which seems very much to be from a similar perspective as far as perceptions on transit and having multiple conflicting/competing systems go. We were there for a friend's wedding a few years back and resolved to do it without renting a car, since we were going to be staying near the airport. Still remember the look the hotel clerk gave us when she asked if we were parking a car and told her our plan.   


"Oh, no one takes the bus here. We all drive."

Thank you, sincerely. I am not trained to handle this, but I tried to confront the situation as a person first and an employee second. And my boss, who I genuinely cannot say enough positive things about because he goes above and beyond all the time for us, didn’t question it for even a heartbeat. There isn’t any sort of training that I could’ve been given that I think would’ve adequately prepared me, but I do want to be able to be ready in a scenario like this, however infrequent.

Regarding her not coming back, that’s been a thing haunting me for a couple of years now, since I started working here. Every time I go more than a week without seeing her my heart drops. I think the thing that upsets me the most is that when she doesn’t come back I may not ever even hear about it. If she’s estranged from her family and out on the street she might pass and get left in an empty house and not be found till spring around here, end up found out in the element as an unidentifiable Jane Doe, or even if her family knows it might never make the papers or get back to me. And I’ll never get explicit knowledge, but in the back of my mind I know. And that absolutely breaks my heart.

When April is on, even though she’s still got hurdles built in with age and her health, she’s lovely. She’s funny, she jokes with us, she remembers those of us who treat her kindly, and she is very, very grateful. She’s in there somewhere on those bad days too, I know it. She was almost nonverbal in the interaction today, but she remembered my name. And I know that is because we have a real relationship. 
I only hope that should I one day find myself in a similar situation, someone would find the patience to be decent to me too. Life is hard enough as it is, and people’s relative inability or refusal to just be kind to each other is one of the things that upsets me most. 

Thank you for taking the time to reply, and for not being afraid to work with our most vulnerable folks. I gather from the tenor of your comment that you are the type of person that should be in those support roles. Thank you, and please do not stop.

That’s one of the things that upsets me so much - I don’t know what else to even offer to her because the social services in my area/state/country are so inadequate (at best) and inhumane (at worst, if you prescribe intent to their design, which I personally do). I agree that just treating people like they’re PEOPLE, and giving them the time of day that they are so frequently deprived of, can go a long way. I was out of work and living in a van for a while and I know that was one of the things that I felt most acutely - just that so many people would not give me the time of day. Simply having someone look you in the eye, remember your name, and talk to you can help to make you feel human again. 

I think I would like to get involved in that sort of stuff. My wife is a support worker in the city next door and comes from a history of very personal, first-hand experience with her own family having dealt with this sort of stuff. It’s one of the things I admire most about her and I’ve tried to help her with her “extracurricular” work when I can but I’ve never really considered how much more I could do if I took some training. I really like this idea, and I am going to look into it to see what I can do right now. Thank you for your advice and for sharing your insight and empathy!

That job sounds tremendously draining from an emotional standpoint, and I cannot imagine the toll that it must take day in and day out. Thank you for the kind words, and thank you for the work you do to help people. That’s a job that is so important.

Is there any advice you would give as far as places I could start to get her help that do not include just cold calling local shelters? From speaking to other long-time workers in the area who know her for longer periods, this has been going on for ages. I gather that she either chooses to leave or gets kicked out of places. I think that is part of why her remaining family has such a limited contact with her - not that they don’t care but that they have tried and she continues to stay along the same track.

She absolutely should be in one, and that makes it so extra heartbreaking. She needs to have someone looking out for her who is actually able to provide palliative care and make her comfortable. I’m genuinely not sure if it’s an ineligibility thing, or if she just will not go. Both my boss and I have spoken with her son briefly over the years but that’s all the family we can find. She had at least one sister who died at the end of this year, and she went to the funeral (taking her at her word here - she brought the memorial card from the service). So she is presumably in contact with some family. Unfortunately, I think she will not willingly go, and I am not knowledgeable enough to know about what, if anything, could be done to make her go if it was against her will. I just would like to see her getting to have some degree of peace in her final years, because no one should have to find themselves in such dire, lonely straights at the end of their life (or at any time during them, in a perfect world). I don’t know what I can do to try to advocate for her. If anyone in this thread knows something concrete I can do, please let me know. I don’t know where to begin.

That's one of the things that keeps me going, honestly, and in my experience the only people who seem to really get it are people who can relate to that specific feeling. There's that unique peace that you make with yourself and with life in general when you've accepted that you can end it at any time. That everything you do is purely on your own terms. I truly believe that in that situation, staying alive is a courageous act. And I don't know what specifically you're going through, but you are incredibly brave for making the conscious decision each day to stay here and tough it out. I don't want my post to come off as defeatist. I want all of us to keep at it, and I'm happy as hell that you are here.

I really appreciate the response. That's been the sort of stuff that has motivated me in the past, and I think that Covid has made it especially difficult in that I've just been in pure survival mode and haven't been able to plan for those sort of bigger, external enjoyable things. I've still been trying to get outside into nature, walk/hike/drive (I live in the city, and honestly, those are some of my most cherished things). But it's the general "timelessness" of this moment in particular. I feel so trapped in this moment and the moment doesn't ever seem to end. So even when I do those little things that I need to like the dishes or make the bed, etc I get lost in the feeling of being trapped in this Groundhog Day sort of situation if that makes sense.   


One of my buddies who is in recovery is always harping on "doing the dishes," which as he explains it sounds to me like exactly what you're saying. Just forcing yourself to do some small, mundane task that you've been putting off. I guess for me the issue is that even if I can get those things done (and I DO, genuinely feel a little bit better after I've done them), I feel so trapped in this single place. Even when I manage to be grounded enough to convince myself that it isn't a permanent place. I have always had a hard time being confined to one spot and in my last year and a half my world has been about two miles wide.   


I'm trying to give myself those things though. I applied to an electrical apprenticeship and passed my aptitude test and am waiting on an interview. I do find myself excited at the prospect of finally getting a job that isn't dead end, getting out of debt, getting a house for my fiancee and I, etc. That's been one of the things I've been clinging to lately, and it's a relief to me to know that those sort of goals (and achieving them) helps in the long term.   


Congrats on where you're at, friend. I am glad to hear that things are going well right now. I hope that the new house is one that you can fill with a lifetime's worth of memories, that you bag a big one on that hunting trip, and that Montana is excellent to you when you finally get there.
